title: Guidance reform: participation, judicial review, and regulatory beneficiaries
shortTitle: Guidance reform: participation, judicial review, and regulatory beneficiaries
summary: The readings debate how to preserve useful guidance while providing affected people a meaningful opportunity to challenge its content.
notes:
Elliott proposes treating an agency’s unpromulgated policy as nonbinding and requiring fresh justification when the agency applies it. The agency could choose between the expense of legislative rulemaking and later case-specific justification. Franklin criticizes this approach because deregulatory guidance may produce no enforcement case in which beneficiaries could contest it. Mendelson also emphasizes that informal processes and enforcement litigation often give regulated parties greater access than beneficiaries. These are competing proposals, not a single judicial test.

Parrillo’s empirical account describes voluntary participation in guidance, including draft publication, stakeholder meetings, and advisory committees. He distinguishes the FDA’s broad guidance procedures from OMB’s narrower economically significant category and explains why guidance consultations generally require lighter analysis and response than legislative rulemaking. Participation can improve information and legitimacy but uses time and staff. Broad procedural mandates can leave documents indefinitely in draft; parties may nevertheless follow them, obscuring whether the agency endorses the text or remains internally divided. Raso’s cited work questions the assumption that agencies systematically choose guidance to evade procedure. The account reports the historical practices described in the assigned reading without representing an audit of present executive guidance policies.
